docs.title: Before every push: sanitization checklist
docs.text:
Compose files often hardcode secrets in environment: blocks. The collector only blanks .env files, so check compose files by hand.

  • [ ] No passwords, API keys, tunnel tokens, webhook URLs, app passwords
  • [ ] Hardcoded environment: secrets moved to .env and referenced as ${VAR}
  • [ ] Decide on internal IPs, usernames, emails, subdomains (redact if public)
  • [ ] No other people's personal details: friends' names, gamertags, or anything named after someone (a modpack, a world, a server)
  • [ ] gitleaks detect --source . -v comes back clean
  • [ ] git status shows no .env, database or data folders

If a secret ever gets pushed: rotate it first, then clean history. Deleting the file is not enough.

docs.title: Incident: a friend's name in a public repo
docs.text: In October 2026 I found a friend's name in this public repo. Removing it took a history rewrite and, in the end, deleting and recreating the repository, which had 33 commits at the time.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text: While reviewing the docs, I noticed the Terraria page named the server's modpack, and the modpack was named after a friend. It had been there since the very first commit, in four slightly different lines across the page's versions. Gitleaks didn't catch it, because it isn't a secret: it's personal information about someone else, which no secret scanner looks for.

docs.title: How it was removed
docs.text:
1. edit the page     → name gone from today's files, but still in every old commit
2. rewrite history   → all 33 commits rewritten, force-pushed
3. check GitHub      → still reachable through pull-request refs and cached commits
4. recreate the repo → the only way to remove those for good
Step What I did Why it wasn't enough on its own 1. Edit the file Replaced the name with "custom modpack" and pushed Git keeps every version. Anyone could click back through old commits and read it. 2. Rewrite history Backed up the repo first, then ran git filter-branch over all 33 commits to replace the name in every version of every file. Checked that no commit still contained it, and that today's files were identical to before. Force-pushed. GitHub keeps pull request refs (refs/pull/1, refs/pull/2) that point at old commits, and owners can't delete them. Old commits also stayed viewable by their ID. 3. Check the live site The docs site is rebuilt from scratch on every push, so it was already clean 4. Recreate the repo Saved every setting (description, topics, Pages, workflow permissions), deleted the repository, recreated it and pushed the clean history This is the only step that removes the PR refs and cached commits. The cost: the record of two closed pull requests.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Git never forgets by default. Deleting a line only hides it from the latest version.
  • Secret scanners don't catch personal information. Names, gamertags and nicknames need a human review, so they're now on the checklist above.
  • Force-pushing isn't the end on GitHub. Pull request refs and cached commits keep old history reachable, so a full cleanup can mean recreating the repository (or asking GitHub Support).
  • Back up before rewriting history, and check the result: the rewrite was confirmed by searching every commit and by comparing the final files byte for byte.
  • Other people's privacy counts too. My friends didn't choose to be in my portfolio.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Nightly, encrypted, deduplicated, self-verifying backups of the data I can't replace, with a tested restore

Tool restic 0.19.1 (single binary, checksum-verified on install) Schedule Nightly at 03:30 (an hour after Immich's own 02:00 database dump) Destination Encrypted restic repository on the NAS's second physical disk Script scripts/homelab-backup.sh Also covers ShineoriServer's apps, through an append-only backup server (details below) Status 🟡 Copy 2 of 3 done. Off-device and off-site copies are next.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: While documenting the lab, I discovered there were no backups at all. I had planned an rsync job but never set it up. My password vault (every login, 2FA code and passkey, for me and the friends I'd invited) and my photo library each existed in exactly one place. Every security fix I'd made that day protected against attackers. Backups protect against what happens to everyone: dead disks, bad updates and mistyped commands.

docs.title: What gets backed up
docs.text: Data How Why this way Vaultwarden database A consistent snapshot with SQLite's online-backup API, then PRAGMA integrity_check The database is in WAL mode and constantly being written. Copying the file directly can produce a corrupt backup that looks fine. Vaultwarden rsa_key* Copied Signs login tokens. Without it, a restored vault can't issue logins. Vaultwarden attachments / sends Copied User files Immich library (originals, profiles) Backed up directly Irreplaceable photos Immich database Immich's own nightly pg_dump (in library/backups/) Copying a live Postgres data folder is unsafe. A logical dump is. Excluded: Immich thumbnails + transcoded video Regenerable, and would only bloat the backups

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    cron([cron 03:30]) --> s[homelab-backup.sh]
    s --> v[Vaultwarden<br/>SQLite online backup<br/>+ integrity check]
    s --> i[Immich library<br/>+ nightly DB dump]
    v --> r[(restic repo<br/>second disk<br/>encrypted · deduplicated)]
    i --> r
    r --> k[forget/prune<br/>7 daily · 4 weekly · 6 monthly]
    k --> c[restic check<br/>re-reads 5% of data]
    s -. any failure .-> d([📱 Discord alert])
Design choice Why Encrypted (restic repository password) A stolen or discarded disk is useless without it. The password is stored in my vault and on paper, because if the vault is what I need to restore, I can't look the password up in it. Deduplicated Nightly runs only store what changed. The first run was 2.3 GiB, and later runs add a few MiB. Retention: 7 daily, 4 weekly, 6 monthly I can go back in time, for example to before a bad update corrupted something Verifies itself nightly restic check --read-data-subset=5% proves the stored data can still be read back Fails loudly An ERR trap sends a Discord alert. Silent backup failure is how people lose data. No secrets in arguments The Discord webhook reaches curl through stdin, never the command line (a lesson from my auditd script) Plaintext staging is deleted The temporary vault snapshot is removed after backup, and also on failure (via the trap) Overlap lock (flock) A slow run can never collide with the next one Installed from GitHub with checksum verification Docker Hub's anonymous pull limit blocked the container image, so I installed the official binary and verified it against the release's SHA256SUMS

docs.title: The restore test ✅
docs.text:
A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a backup.

On the first night, I restored from the backup into a scratch folder and compared it against the live data:

restored DB integrity:  ok
users    backup=  4   live=  4
ciphers  backup=548   live=548     (every vault item accounted for)
rsa_key identical:      YES
immich DB dump restorable: YES     (gzip integrity verified)

Then I deleted the scratch copy, since it contained a plaintext vault database.

docs.title: The failure-alert test ✅
docs.text:
An alert I've never seen fire is no better than an untested backup. So I ran a throwaway copy of the script pointed at a repository that doesn't exist:

Fatal: repository does not exist        ← deliberate failure
exit code: 1                            ← failure detected
staging folder: 0 files                 ← plaintext vault snapshot cleaned up anyway
📱 Discord #backups: "❌ ShiNAS backup FAILED (line …)"   ← failure reported

One test proved all three: failures are detected, reported, and cleaned up after. Alerts go to a dedicated #backups channel with its own webhook, stored root-only and passed to curl over stdin.

docs.title: How to restore 📖
docs.text: A runbook for future me, written while everything still works.

docs.title: How the password works
docs.text:
restic encrypts everything before it's written to disk. The repository password unlocks the repository's key, which decrypts the data. Without it, the repository is unreadable, by anyone, including me. There's no recovery option.

password ──▶ unlocks the repository key ──▶ decrypts the backups
Where the password lives Used when /root/.restic-password (root-only file on the NAS) Automatically, every night. I never type it. 🔐 My vault + 📝 a paper copy Disaster only: the NAS was reinstalled, the file is gone, or the backup disk moved to another machine

docs.title: Setup for every command below (on the NAS)
docs.text:
export RESTIC_REPOSITORY=/volume2/backups/restic
export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE=/root/.restic-password   # skip this line to be prompted for the password instead
sudo -E restic snapshots                              # the timeline of every backup

docs.title: Scenario A: get back a single file or an older version 🙂
docs.text:
sudo -E restic restore latest --tag vaultwarden --target /tmp/restore   # or a snapshot ID instead of "latest"
# ...copy what you need out of /tmp/restore, then:
sudo rm -rf /tmp/restore

Or browse backups like normal folders:

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/restic && sudo -E restic mount /mnt/restic
# in another terminal: ls /mnt/restic/snapshots/     (Ctrl+C in the first terminal to unmount)

docs.title: Scenario B: restore Vaultwarden completely 🔑
docs.text:
sudo -E restic restore latest --tag vaultwarden --target /tmp/restore
cd ~/docker/vaultwarden && sudo docker compose stop          # nothing writes during the swap
sudo cp -a vw-data vw-data.before-restore                    # safety copy of the current state
sudo cp -a /tmp/restore/volume2/backups/staging/vaultwarden/. vw-data/
sudo docker compose start && sudo rm -rf /tmp/restore

The backup includes the database, rsa_key* (without it, existing logins break) and attachments. Check by logging in and confirming your item count.

docs.title: Scenario C: restore Immich 📸
docs.text:
1. Restore the library: sudo -E restic restore latest --tag immich --target /tmp/restore, then copy .../immich/library/ back into place with the stack stopped
  2. The database comes back from the newest dump in library/backups/*.sql.gz, following Immich's official restore procedure for the installed version (it loads the dump into a fresh, empty database container). Thumbnails regenerate on their own afterwards.

docs.title: Scenario D: total disaster 💥 (NAS dead or reinstalled)
docs.text:
1. Get the backup disk mounted on a working Linux machine (or a reinstalled NAS)
  2. Install restic from GitHub and verify it with sha256sum -c against the release's SHA256SUMS
  3. restic -r /path/to/backups/restic snapshots, and type the password from paper / the vault at the prompt
  4. Continue with Scenarios B and C

⚠️ If the NAS and its disks are lost (fire, theft, ransomware), this repository is gone too. That's why off-device and off-site copies are next on the roadmap.

docs.title: ShineoriServer backups (append-only)
docs.text:
After moving six services to my laptop server, their data sat outside the nightly backup. The laptop now backs up to the NAS, designed so that the laptop can add backups but can never delete them.

flowchart LR
    cron([cron 04:15<br/>laptop]) --> s[laptop-backup.sh]
    s --> d[Dawarich<br/>pg_dump + pg_restore --list]
    s --> p[Uptime Kuma, Homarr, Karakeep<br/>paused ~3 s for a consistent copy]
    d --> r[restic<br/>encrypts on the laptop]
    p --> r
    r -- HTTP over LAN --> rs[rest-server on ShiNAS<br/>--append-only --private-repos]
    rs --> repo[(second disk<br/>separate repository)]
    nas([cron Sun 05:00<br/>ShiNAS]) --> pr[laptop-backup-prune.sh<br/>forget/prune + check]
    pr --> repo
    s -. any failure .-> dc([📱 Discord alert])
    pr -. any failure .-> dc
What Dawarich (database dump + its files), Karakeep (data volume), Uptime Kuma, Homarr, plus each app's compose file and .env Not included Karakeep's search index (rebuildable), AI models (re-downloadable), the Minecraft world (it has its own daily backup) Schedule Laptop nightly at 04:15, after the NAS's own 03:30 run so they don't compete for the disk. NAS cleanup Sundays at 05:00. Scripts laptop-backup.sh on the laptop, laptop-backup-prune.sh on the NAS Backup server stacks/restic-server/, bound to the NAS's LAN IP Size First run: 340 MiB of data, 167 MiB stored after compression Design decision Why Append-only backup server The laptop's login can only add data. If the laptop were ever compromised, by ransomware for example, the attacker couldn't delete or overwrite its backups. Cleanup runs on the NAS, directly on the files, where the laptop has no say. Encrypted on the laptop The NAS only ever receives encrypted data --private-repos The laptop's login can only reach its own repository A separate repository The NAS's backups and the laptop's can't affect each other pg_dump for Dawarich, a short pause for the SQLite apps Both give a consistent copy. PostgreSQL can dump while it runs. For the small SQLite apps, stopping them for about 3 seconds is simpler and more reliable than locating every database file. An EXIT trap restarts them even if the backup fails. Secrets in root-only files The server login lives in a chmod 600 repository file and the encryption key in a chmod 600 password file. Both were typed with read -s, so neither appeared on screen or in shell history. The key is also in my password manager.

docs.title: Proven ✅
docs.text: Test Result Restore Restored the Dawarich dump from the NAS and read it with pg_restore --list: database dawarich_development, 578 entries Delete from the laptop restic forget <snapshot> was refused by the NAS with 403 Forbidden 🔒 Cleanup + verification on the NAS Retention applied, and restic check re-read 5% of the data: no errors were found Key in my password manager Its SHA-256 fingerprint matches the key the backups actually use, checked without displaying the key

docs.title: Restoring a ShineoriServer app
docs.text:
On the laptop:

R="sudo RESTIC_REPOSITORY_FILE=/root/.restic-repo RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE=/root/.restic-password restic"
$R snapshots
$R restore latest --target /tmp/restore --include /home/shineori/docker/uptime-kuma    # one app's folder

If the laptop is gone, run restic on the NAS against /volume2/backups/restic-laptop/shineoriserver, using the encryption key from my password manager. The Dawarich database comes back from var/backups/homelab-staging/dawarich.dump with pg_restore into a fresh Dawarich (listing it is tested; a full database reload is on the drill list below).

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Problem Root cause Fix toomanyrequests pulling the restic image Docker Hub's anonymous pull limit, after a night of image pulls Installed the official binary from GitHub instead, verified with sha256sum -c The script got scrambled when pasted into the terminal A long multi-line paste was mangled by the terminal Delivered the file over the network share instead, and confirmed it with a matching SHA-256 on both ends The restore test couldn't find the restored Immich dump My test made the folder root-only, but the *.sql.gz wildcard was expanded by my user shell before sudo ran Ran the whole check inside sudo sh -c '...'. The backup itself was fine. The NAS cleanup failed: wrong password or no key found The key I typed on the NAS didn't match the laptop's (a paste slip) Compared SHA-256 fingerprints of both files without showing either key, then copied the laptop's working file over SSH instead of retyping it. Also checked that my password manager's copy matched. A restore check said Permission denied even with sudo In sudo cmd < file, the < is handled by my own shell, not by root sudo sh -c 'cmd < file', so root opens the file

docs.title: Roadmap to full 3-2-1
docs.text:
• [x] Copy 1: live data on the NAS
  • [x] Copy 2: encrypted restic repository on a separate physical disk (survives a dead drive or a bad command)
  • [ ] Copy 3, separate device: replicate the repository to my second server, so the backups survive the whole NAS dying
  • [ ] Off-site: encrypted copy to cloud storage, so the backups survive fire, theft or ransomware on the home network
  • [x] Back up ShineoriServer too ✅ Done: nightly, encrypted, append-only backups to the NAS, with a tested restore (above)
  • [ ] Dead-man's switch: an Uptime Kuma push monitor that alerts if a night's backup doesn't run at all (the Discord trap only catches runs that start and then fail)
  • [ ] Add Paperless (scanned documents are as irreplaceable as photos): its data/ and media/ folders, or a nightly document_exporter run
  • [ ] Quarterly restore drill, including a full reload of the Dawarich database into a test container

docs.title: Moving services off the NAS
docs.text:
My NAS ran out of RAM, so I moved six services to my second server without losing any data, and documented every snag along the way.

From ShiNAS (NAS appliance, 7.5 GB RAM) To ShineoriServer (repurposed laptop, 31 GB RAM, RTX 2060) Moved Immich machine learning, Uptime Kuma, Homarr, Dawarich, Karakeep, Ghiro When October 2026

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The night before, the NAS overloaded: load average 36, swap almost full, and every app timing out (the full diagnosis is in the Immich troubleshooting log). Capping Immich's machine-learning container fixed the crash, but the NAS was still tight:

ShiNAS: 7.5 GB total
├─ containers     ≈ 2.9 GB  (measured with docker stats)
├─ NAS system     ≈ 2.4 GB
├─ disk cache     ≈ 2.8 GB  (given back when apps need it)
└─ available      ≈ 2.2 GB  ← one ML job (up to 2 GB) or a video transcode used all of it

Meanwhile the laptop server had 31 GB of RAM and was mostly idle between AI chats.

docs.title: How I chose what moves
docs.text:
📦 Big, irreplaceable data stays on the NAS. Apps that need lots of RAM but hold little data move.

Stays on ShiNAS 🔒 Why Immich (server + database), Paperless Irreplaceable photos and documents. Immich is in the nightly encrypted backup; adding Paperless is on the backup roadmap. Vaultwarden, Authentik Identity and passwords: the most important services stay on the most reliable box Jellyfin, Audiobookshelf, *arr stack, qBittorrent They read and write the media on the NAS disks directly Diun, resume site, cloudflared Diun watches the host it runs on; the other two are tiny Moved to ShineoriServer 🚚 RAM on the NAS (idle) Data Immich machine learning up to 2 GB during jobs none (model files only) Dawarich (4 containers) ~450 MiB small Postgres database Homarr ~260 MiB one small folder Uptime Kuma ~160 MiB one SQLite file Karakeep headless Chrome + search engine small Ghiro only while running none

Uptime Kuma had a second reason: a monitor running on the box it watches can't warn you when that box dies. During the overload it went down with the NAS instead of reporting it. Now it watches the NAS from outside, including a ping monitor for the NAS itself.

docs.title: How each one moved
docs.text:
Every move followed the same safety rule: copy, start on the laptop, check, and only then switch traffic. The NAS copy stayed untouched as a one-command rollback.

NAS: stop app ─▶ pack data ─▶ copy over SSH ─▶ laptop: unpack ─▶ start ─▶ check ─▶ repoint tunnel + monitors
                                                                                   (NAS copy kept for rollback)
Service Method The interesting part Immich ML Nothing to copy Immich can send ML work to another machine by URL. The NAS keeps the service definition behind a compose profiles: switch, so rolling back is one line. Uptime Kuma Folder copy Stopped first, so SQLite's write-ahead log (kuma.db-wal) was merged into the database before copying Homarr Folder copy, including .env The .env holds the encryption key for every saved integration secret. Without it, they come back unreadable. Dawarich Docker volume export and import Its data lives in 5 Docker named volumes, not in its folder, so copying the folder alone would have produced an empty Dawarich. I exported each volume to a tarball with a throwaway container, then imported them into fresh volumes on the laptop. Karakeep Volume export and import A port clash (Open WebUI already had 3000) and a dead image registry. See below. Ghiro Fresh install It had no data, and the old image turned out to be damaged

The volume trick, for reference:

# export (NAS): read the volume with an image that's already downloaded, so nothing new is pulled
docker run --rm --entrypoint tar -v dawarich_dawarich_db_data:/v:ro -v /tmp/move:/out \
  postgis/postgis:17-3.5-alpine czf /out/db_data.tgz -C /v .

# import (laptop): `docker compose create` makes the empty volumes, then fill them
docker run --rm --entrypoint tar -v dawarich_dawarich_db_data:/v -v ~/docker/move:/in \
  postgis/postgis:17-3.5-alpine xzf /in/db_data.tgz -C /v

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Problem Root cause Fix The laptop couldn't download anything: lookup ghcr.io ... i/o timeout Not DNS. The laptop could reach the router but not the internet. A host-wide ProtonVPN WireGuard tunnel (wg-quick@proton) was sending all traffic into a tunnel that had stopped passing traffic. It hid from ip route because WireGuard uses separate policy-routing rules (ip rule). SearXNG already had its own VPN through gluetun, so the host-wide tunnel was redundant (a VPN inside a VPN). Brought it down and disabled it at boot. scp from the NAS said No such file or directory for a file that existed Newer scp uses SFTP, and the NAS locks SFTP into the shared folders, so its /tmp isn't the real /tmp Streamed the file over plain SSH instead: ssh nas 'cat /tmp/file.tgz' > file.tgz Karakeep's headless-Chrome image wouldn't download: billing must be enabled The Google registry project hosting it stopped serving downloads. The NAS only had it because it was downloaded long ago. Switched to the same image on Docker Hub (docker.io/zenika/alpine-chrome:124) Karakeep's NEXTAUTH_URL was http://localhost:3000 A wrong value from the original setup, found while moving it Set it to the public hostname Dawarich login ended on a Cloudflare 502 The tunnel route still pointed at the NAS, and I had started the login on the laptop's IP while Authentik returns you to the public hostname Repointed the route; logins start from the public hostname Homarr's Uptime Kuma widget returned 404 With "no secrets", Homarr reads a status page with the slug default, which didn't exist Created a status page and entered its slug Homarr's tile still opened the old address In Homarr, the integration (data for widgets) and the app (where the tile links) are stored separately Updated the app's URL as well docker save of Ghiro failed: a file missing from an image layer The locally built image on the NAS was damaged, and its Dockerfile is based on long-retired Ubuntu 16.04 and Python 2 It held no data, so: built fresh on the laptop first, then removed everything from the NAS (docker compose down -v --rmi all)

├─ Uptime Kuma  (watches the NAS)         ├─ Vaultwarden, Authentik  (identity)

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Know where your data actually lives. A folder copy is enough for bind mounts; named volumes need an export. Checking docker volume ls first saved me from moving an empty app.

  • Read the routing table and the rules. ip route looked normal while WireGuard's policy rules sent everything into a dead tunnel.

docs.title: Minecraft world backups
docs.text:
Daily world snapshots that skip quiet days, keep 5 recent copies on the game server, and archive every older copy to the NAS before it's deleted

Host ShineoriServer (runs the backup), ShiNAS (long-term archive) Category Backups Status 🟢 running Schedule Daily at 04:30 (root cron on ShineoriServer) Script scripts/mc-backup.sh Size About 450 MB per snapshot (compressed .tar.gz)

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text:
The Minecraft server world wasn't in my nightly restic backups, and I'd already had to start the world over once after server problems. A world is weeks of my friends' building, so I wanted:

  • A copy for every day something actually happened, without filling the disk with identical copies on days nobody played
  • A few recent copies close by on the game server, for fast restores
  • Every older copy kept forever on the NAS, so nothing is lost when the local copies rotate out

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    cron([cron 04:30<br/>ShineoriServer]) --> flush[RCON: save-off<br/>save-all flush]
    flush --> fp{World changed?<br/>fingerprint vs last run}
    fp -- no --> skip([Skip, nothing to do])
    fp -- yes --> tar[tar.gz the world folder<br/>written as .part, then renamed]
    tar --> on[RCON: save-on]
    skip --> rot
    on --> rot{More than 5<br/>local backups?}
    rot -- no --> done([Done])
    rot -- yes --> up[Stream oldest to ShiNAS<br/>over a plain SSH command]
    up --> ver{SHA-256 matches<br/>on both ends?}
    ver -- yes --> del[Rename on NAS,<br/>delete local copy]
    ver -- no --> keep([Keep local copy,<br/>retry next run])
Piece Job mc-backup.sh One bash script, run by root's crontab on ShineoriServer RCON (rcon-cli inside the container) Pauses autosave and flushes everything in memory to disk, so the copy is consistent Fingerprint A SHA-256 of every world file's path, size and modified time. If it matches the last backup's, nothing changed Local store ~/backups/minecraft on ShineoriServer, newest 5 snapshots plus backup.log Archive ~/backups/minecraft on ShiNAS, grows forever Dedicated SSH key A root-only, passphrase-less key used only for this job

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Delete only after a verified copy The local file is removed only after the NAS copy's SHA-256 matches. A failed or partial transfer can never cost me a backup Upload as .part, rename after verifying A half-finished upload can never look like a real backup on the NAS Dedicated SSH key for the job It's separate from my personal key, so I can revoke it without touching my own access BatchMode=yes on every SSH call The script fails instead of hanging on a password or host-key prompt at 4:30 AM Autosave always turned back on A trap runs save-on even if the script crashes halfway, so the server never keeps running with saving disabled flock overlap lock A slow run can never collide with the next one No NAS address in this repo The published script uses a <nas-lan-ip> placeholder Relies on the server's existing protections RCON stays inside the container (the port isn't published), and the server pauses when empty, which also keeps quiet days from looking "changed"

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Copy the script to /usr/local/bin/mc-backup.sh and chmod +x it. Check the config block at the top: the data folder, the world folder name (it matches level-name in server.properties, not "world"), and the NAS path
  2. Give root its own key to the NAS: 
    sudo ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /root/.ssh/nas_backup -N ""
sudo ssh-copy-id -i /root/.ssh/nas_backup.pub shineori@<nas>
sudo ssh -i /root/.ssh/nas_backup shineori@<nas> "echo it works"   # also saves the host key for root
  3. On the NAS, make sure ~/backups/minecraft is owned by my user, not root: sudo chown -R shineori: ~/backups
  4. Test run, then run it again right away. The second run should log No changes since last backup, skipping.
  5. Schedule it: sudo crontab -e, then add 30 4 * * * /usr/local/bin/mc-backup.sh
  6. Test the NAS handoff without waiting a week: touch 5 empty fake backups named world_2000-01-0X_0000.tar.gz, run the script, and check that the oldest fake shows up on the NAS. Then delete the fakes on both machines

Restoring: stop the container, move the broken world folder aside, then tar -xzf world_<date>.tar.gz -C ~/docker/minecraft/mc-data and start the container again. Older snapshots come from the NAS first.

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Date Problem Root cause Fix 2026-10 First draft would have backed up the wrong folder Assumed the world was data/world, but the data folder is mc-data and the world is named after level-name Checked server.properties and ls mc-data, then fixed both paths 2026-10 A backup was made every run, even with nobody online save-all rewrites level.dat on every save, which changed the fingerprint Ignore level.dat and level.dat_old in the fingerprint (they're still in the backup) 2026-10 Still backing up with nobody online. I suspected Chunky Listed files newer than the last backup with find -newer: zero terrain files changed, but 64 files in entities/ did. The server re-saves entity data on its own Ignore */entities/* in the fingerprint. Real play still trips it through players/, terrain, data/ and poi/ 2026-10 rsync to the NAS: connection unexpectedly closed (0 bytes received) The NAS vendor replaces rsync with a wrapper that tries to become root and only accepts its own shared-folder paths (invalid path). Running rsync by hand with -v showed the real error Stopped using rsync for the transfer 2026-10 scp: No such file or directory for a folder that clearly existed Modern scp uses SFTP, and the NAS's SFTP server is also replaced and maps paths differently from the real shell Stream the file through a plain SSH command (ssh ... "cat > file.part" < file), which sees the real filesystem 2026-10 Permission denied writing the .part file The archive folder on the NAS was owned by root, but the job logs in as my user sudo chown -R shineori: ~/backups, confirmed with a touch test

docs.text:
• [ ] Discord alert on failure (an ERR trap like my restic backups), so a broken night doesn't go unnoticed
  • [ ] Uptime Kuma push monitor as a dead-man's switch, in case the job stops running entirely
  • [ ] Restrict the NAS key in authorized_keys so it can only run the few commands this job needs
  • [ ] Do a real restore drill into a test container, not just the copy test
  • [ ] A size or age limit on the NAS archive, or move it into restic for deduplication (each snapshot is a full 450 MB copy right now)
  • [ ] Include the server config and mods folder, not just the world, so a full rebuild needs only the backup

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Debug from evidence, not guesses: find -newer turned "it must be Chunky" into a file list that pointed somewhere else completely
  • "Changed" is harder to define than it sounds: a game server touches files on its own, so I had to decide which files mean a player did something
  • Appliance NAS tools aren't stock Linux: its rsync and SFTP are replaced with vendor versions, while a plain SSH shell still behaves normally
  • Test the failure path on purpose: fake old backups proved the NAS handoff in minutes instead of a week, and the failed attempts proved the script keeps local copies when something breaks
  • Run the same command by hand with more output: rsync -v showed the real error that the script's log was hiding
  • Ownership matters on both ends: SSH working doesn't mean the remote user can write to the folder

docs.title: *arr stack
docs.text:
Prowlarr + arr apps + qBittorrent routed through gluetun/ProtonVPN

Host ShiNAS Category Media Status 🟢 running Exposed? LAN only; torrent traffic leaves through ProtonVPN (gluetun)

Compose file: stacks/arr-stack/

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text: It automates my media library: I request a show or movie, and the stack finds it, downloads it and files it where Jellyfin picks it up. The important part is that all download traffic goes through a VPN, with a kill switch so it can never leak out over my home IP.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Almost every app shares one network stack: gluetun's. They have no network of their own, so if the VPN drops, they simply can't reach the internet.

flowchart LR
    me([Me, on the LAN]) --> seerr[Jellyseerr<br/>requests :5055]
    seerr --> g
    subgraph g[gluetun network stack · ProtonVPN]
        prowlarr[Prowlarr<br/>indexers]
        fs[FlareSolverr]
        sonarr[Sonarr · TV]
        radarr[Radarr · movies]
        lidarr[Lidarr · music]
        qb[qBittorrent]
    end
    g --> vpn{{ProtonVPN tunnel}} --> net((Internet))
    sync[qb_port_sync] -. forwarded port .-> qb
    qb --> data[(/volume1/data)]
    sonarr --> data
    radarr --> data
    data --> jf[Jellyfin]
Container Job gluetun The VPN client. Owns the network stack every other app uses. Its firewall only opens the ports listed in FIREWALL_INPUT_PORTS. Prowlarr + FlareSolverr Manage the indexers (search sources); FlareSolverr gets past their bot-check pages Sonarr / Radarr / Lidarr Watch for TV, movies and music, send downloads to qBittorrent, then rename and file the results qBittorrent The download client qb_port_sync A small curl loop: gluetun gets a forwarded port from ProtonVPN, and this pushes it into qBittorrent's settings whenever it changes Jellyseerr The request page. It sits outside the VPN because it only talks to Jellyfin and the arr apps, not to the internet.

One shared /volume1/data mount for qBittorrent and the arr apps means a finished download can be moved or hard-linked into the library instantly, instead of being copied.

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why network_mode: "service:gluetun" Built-in kill switch: VPN down means no traffic at all, never a fallback to my home IP ProtonVPN port forwarding + automatic sync Incoming peers can connect, without me opening any port on the router LAN only None of these apps are published through the tunnel Credentials in a git-ignored .env VPN and qBittorrent passwords; the repo only has a blanked .env.example Pinned images Every app pinned to a version (gluetun by digest) and announced by Diun

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Fill .env: TZ, PUID/PGID, the ProtonVPN OpenVPN username (with +pmp for port forwarding) and password, and the qBittorrent Web UI login
  2. Every app that uses network_mode: service:gluetun publishes its port on gluetun, and that port must also be in FIREWALL_INPUT_PORTS
  3. docker compose up -d, then check gluetun's logs for the VPN connection and the forwarded port
  4. In the arr apps, the download client and each other are at gluetun:<port>, because they all share that container's network
  5. Jellyseerr connects to Jellyfin and to Sonarr/Radarr

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Date Problem Root cause Fix — qBittorrent could refuse to start after an unclean shutdown A stale lockfile left in its config folder The container's entrypoint deletes the lockfile before starting — The forwarded port changes whenever the VPN reconnects, breaking incoming connections ProtonVPN assigns a new port each session Added the qb_port_sync sidecar, which updates qBittorrent automatically 2026-10-11 Every arr app went down at the same moment The whole NAS was overloaded by Immich, not a problem in this stack (diagnosis) Fixed the overload and moved RAM-heavy apps to my second server; the stack is back up

docs.text:

  • [ ] Pin the curlimages/curl image used by qb_port_sync
  • [ ] Put the qBittorrent password in a file instead of an environment variable

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Sharing a network namespace is a simple, reliable kill switch: no VPN, no network
  • VPN port forwarding and why a dynamic port needs automation
  • Hard links and atomic moves only work when the download and library folders are on the same mount
  • Small sidecar containers can glue two apps together without changing either one

docs.title: Authentik
docs.text:
Single sign-on and identity provider for the lab, with passwordless passkey login

Host ShiNAS Category Security & identity Status 🟢 running Exposed? Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports) Version 2026.8.3 (pinned)

Compose file: stacks/authentik/

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text: Password fatigue. As the lab grew, every app came with its own login page, its own account and its own password to manage. That meant more passwords to rotate and more front doors to secure. Authentik replaced that with one identity: a single account, unlocked with a passkey, that my apps trust through OpenID Connect (OIDC). It's the same pattern companies use with Okta or Entra ID, just running on my own hardware.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    me([Me + browser<br/>passkey]) --> cf[Cloudflare edge<br/>HTTPS]
    cf --> tun[cloudflared<br/>host service on ShiNAS]
    tun --> srv[authentik server<br/>:9000 / :9453]
    srv --> db[(PostgreSQL 16)]
    wrk[authentik worker<br/>background tasks + email] --> db
    wrk -. SMTP .-> mail[Dedicated alerts<br/>mailbox]
    immich[Immich] -- OIDC --> srv
    daw[Dawarich] -- OIDC --> srv

How a login works: I open Immich or Dawarich and click "Login with Authentik". The app redirects me to Authentik, I approve with a passkey (no password), and Authentik sends me back with a signed OIDC token that says who I am. The app never sees a password at all.

Container Job server Web UI, login flows, OIDC endpoints worker Background jobs: sending email, cleanup, outpost management postgresql Users, flows, policies, sessions

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Passkeys, no passwords Phishing-resistant. A fake login page can't steal a passkey the way it can steal a password. Published through a Cloudflare Tunnel Zero inbound ports on my router. The tunnel dials out, so there's nothing to port-scan. Renamed the default admin account The default admin username is public knowledge. Renaming it removes half of what an attacker needs. Recovery key kept as break-glass If I ever lose my passkeys, I can generate a one-time recovery link from the server terminal instead of being locked out of my own SSO. SSO is optional in each app Apps keep a local login fallback, so an Authentik outage can't lock me out of everything at once. Dedicated mailbox for outbound email Authentik sends mail through a homelab-only account with an app password, not my personal email. Version pinned Upgrades happen when I choose, after reading the release notes, not by surprise on a restart. Secrets in .env, never in git The repo only has a blanked .env.example. gitleaks scans every push.

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Generate secrets: openssl rand -base64 60 | tr -d '\n' for both AUTHENTIK_SECRET_KEY and PG_PASS, saved to .env (and to Vaultwarden).
  2. Fix the port conflict: set COMPOSE_PORT_HTTPS=9453 in .env (see troubleshooting below). HTTP stays on 9000.
  3. Start it: docker compose up -d, then wait for postgresql to report healthy.
  4. Initial setup: browse to /if/flow/initial-setup/ to create the first admin.
  5. Harden the admin: rename the default admin, enroll a passkey, switch the login flow to passwordless.
  6. Create a break-glass recovery link when needed: docker compose run --rm server create_recovery_key 10 <admin-username>
  7. Add email: fill in the SMTP block in .env and send a test email from the admin UI.
  8. Publish: add a public hostname in the Cloudflare Tunnel config that points to the server's HTTP port.
  9. Connect apps: for each app, create an OAuth2/OpenID provider + application in Authentik, then paste the client ID, client secret and issuer URL into the app.

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Problem Root cause Fix Authentik's HTTPS port wouldn't bind on ShiNAS the NAS's built-in web server (nginx) already listens on 9443, Authentik's default HTTPS port Moved Authentik's HTTPS to 9453 with COMPOSE_PORT_HTTPS in .env. HTTP stays on 9000. Dawarich SSO didn't work with Authentik's default scopes Dawarich is strict about the email claim it receives over OIDC Built a custom email scope mapping that marks the email as verified, and assigned it to the Dawarich provider

docs.text:
• [x] Removed the Docker socket from the worker ✅ Done. The upstream default mounts /var/run/docker.sock so Authentik can deploy outposts, but socket access is effectively root on the host. I only run the built-in embedded outpost, so I removed the mount and verified the running container no longer has it (docker inspect showed 0 socket mounts). Authentik's health checks stayed green.
  • [ ] Drop user: root from the worker. Its data folders were created as root, so this needs a careful ownership fix first.
  • [ ] Add Homarr to SSO (planned)
  • [ ] Automated pg_dump backups of the Authentik database
  • [ ] Authorization policies so each app only accepts the users it should

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• How OIDC actually works: redirects, client IDs and secrets, issuer URLs, scopes and claims. The Dawarich fix taught me that a "scope" is just a bundle of claims, and that I can write my own when an app expects something the defaults don't provide.
  • Passwordless authentication with WebAuthn passkeys, plus planning for the failure case (break-glass recovery).
  • Debugging port conflicts on an appliance OS that reserves ports for its own services.
  • Thinking in tradeoffs: optional SSO keeps things available, the docker socket mount trades security for convenience, and a pinned version trades freshness for stability.

docs.title: Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.text:
The lab's front door: publishes web apps to the internet with zero open ports, with a Zero Trust gate in front of the admin panel

Host ShiNAS (runs as a host service, not in Docker); a second, separate tunnel runs on ShineoriServer (see below) Category Networking & monitoring Status 🟢 running Mode Remotely managed (token): routes live in the Cloudflare dashboard Version Kept current through the package manager, with auto-update disabled

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text:
Opening ports on my home router would put every service, and my home IP address, directly on the internet. A Cloudflare Tunnel flips that around. A small agent (cloudflared) on the NAS dials out to Cloudflare, and visitors reach my apps through Cloudflare's network. So I get:

  • Zero inbound ports. There's nothing on my router for scanners to find.
  • My home IP stays hidden. DNS points at Cloudflare, not at my house.
  • Free HTTPS and DDoS protection at Cloudflare's edge.
  • A place to enforce identity (Cloudflare Access) before traffic ever reaches my network.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    v([Visitor]) --> edge[Cloudflare edge<br/>HTTPS + DDoS]
    edge --> acc{Cloudflare Access<br/>NAS panel only}
    acc -- passkey via Authentik --> tun
    edge --> tun[[Outbound tunnel]]
    tun --> cfd[cloudflared<br/>on ShiNAS]
    cfd --> apps[Web apps on ShiNAS]
    cfd --> ai[Open WebUI, Dawarich, Karakeep<br/>on ShineoriServer]
    edge -. unknown hostname .-> x[404 catch-all]

docs.title: Two tunnels, one per domain
docs.text:
I own two domains, and each one has its own tunnel on its own machine:

Tunnel Runs on Publishes Tunnel 1 (this page) ShiNAS Everything on my main domain, including apps that live on ShineoriServer, reached over the LAN Tunnel 2 ShineoriServer My second domain

Keeping them separate means each tunnel has its own token and its own routes, and a problem with one machine or one tunnel never takes down the other domain.

docs.title: What's published
docs.text: App Runs on Protection in front of the app NAS admin panel ShiNAS 🔐 Cloudflare Access → Authentik passkey, then the NAS login Authentik (the SSO itself) ShiNAS Passkey login (deliberately not behind Access, or logins would loop) Vaultwarden ShiNAS App login (its clients need direct API access) Immich ShiNAS App login, with optional Authentik SSO Dawarich ShineoriServer App login, with optional Authentik SSO Jellyfin, Audiobookshelf ShiNAS App login Karakeep ShineoriServer App login Open WebUI ShineoriServer App login (usually spun down) Any other hostname n/a Catch-all rule returns 404, so nothing unlisted is reachable

docs.text: Traffic Path Why Web apps Cloudflare Tunnel Web traffic is what tunnel routes are built for Game servers (Minecraft) playit.gg Games speak raw TCP/UDP, which tunnel web routes can't carry Flowcase LAN only Doesn't need to be on the internet, so it isn't The Forest server Tailscale Private, friends-only VPN

docs.title: Security audit
docs.text:
When I documented this tunnel, I reviewed every route and DNS record instead of trusting what I thought was configured. It turned up five problems:

Severity Finding Risk Fix Status 🔴 High The NAS admin panel was public. Anyone could reach its login page. NAS admin panels are a top ransomware target. One firmware bug or weak password could expose every file. Put Cloudflare Access in front, using my own Authentik as the identity provider. Strangers are redirected to a login before any traffic reaches the NAS. ✅ Fixed 🟠 Medium A DNS record pointed straight at my home IP. It was left over from an old setup for the Minecraft server. It skipped Cloudflare entirely and published my home address, a DDoS and scanning target. Deleted the record. Friends use playit.gg, which never reveals my IP. ✅ Fixed 🟡 Low A route still pointed at an app I'd removed. Harmless while nothing listens there, but anything I later ran on that port would become public by accident. Deleted the route and its DNS record. ✅ Fixed 🟡 Low A route for game traffic that could never work. Clutter that hides what's really exposed. Deleted. ✅ Fixed 🟡 Low A forgotten dynamic-DNS container on the Minecraft server, configured to publish my home IP on another hostname It had been failing silently for a long time (Cloudflare rejected its API token), but if anyone ever fixed the token, it would start leaking my IP again Suspected it of re-creating the deleted record, but checking its config and logs proved it wasn't the cause. Removed it anyway, along with its credential. ✅ Fixed

docs.title: How the Access gate works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant V as Visitor
    participant CF as Cloudflare Access
    participant AK as Authentik
    participant NAS as NAS panel
    V->>CF: request NAS panel
    CF-->>V: 302: log in first (no session)
    V->>AK: OIDC login with passkey
    AK-->>CF: signed token (email)
    CF->>CF: policy: email = me AND login method = Authentik
    CF->>NAS: allowed, forward through tunnel

Design choices:

  • Default deny. Nothing gets through unless a policy explicitly allows it.
  • Two independent locks in one policy: my email AND logged in through Authentik. If the app's identity-provider setting were ever changed by mistake, the policy alone would still reject any other login method.
  • Least privilege in Authentik: the OIDC app only allows the authorization code and refresh token grants. The password grant is off, so nothing can trade a password for a token and skip my passkey.
  • Bound to one user: only my account is bound to the Cloudflare Access application in Authentik.
  • Fail closed: if the binding check errors, access is denied.
  • Lockout plan: if Authentik or the tunnel is down, I can still reach the panel on my home network.

Verified from outside with no cookies: a request to the NAS panel gets a 302 redirect to the Cloudflare Access login, with auth_status: NONE.

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Create the tunnel in Cloudflare Zero Trust → Networks → Tunnels. Choose the cloudflared connector and copy the install command (it contains the token).
  2. Install on the host: cloudflared service install <token> creates a systemd service that starts on boot.
  3. Keep it updated through the package manager (auto-update is off, so updates happen on my schedule).
  4. Add routes under Published application routes: hostname → http://localhost:<port> (or a LAN address for apps on other machines).
  5. Keep the catch-all at http_status:404.
  6. Check it: systemctl status cloudflared, plus Live logs in the dashboard.

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Problem Root cause Fix Testing the new identity provider showed "Unable to find the requested identity provider" I tested immediately after saving, and the new config hadn't reached Cloudflare's edge yet Waited a minute and ran Test again from the identity-provider list. "Your connection works!" After I deleted the home-IP record, it still resolved The first delete didn't take. I suspected a DDNS updater was re-creating it and found one on another host, but its logs showed it managed a different hostname and had never succeeded Deleted the record again and verified it against Cloudflare's authoritative nameservers, not a cached resolver. Removed the dormant updater anyway. Couldn't find a cloudflared folder with the other Docker stacks The tunnel runs as a host service, not a container. A cloudflared compose file in another stack's folder was an unused install leftover. Documented the real setup: a systemd service in token mode After moving Dawarich to the laptop, Sign in with Authentik ended on a Cloudflare 502 I started the login on the laptop's IP, but Authentik sends you back to the public hostname, and that route still pointed at the NAS, where Dawarich was now stopped Pointed the route at the laptop. Logins now start from the public hostname, so the login cookie and the return address match.

docs.title: What I'd harden next
docs.text:
• [x] Moved the tunnel token out of the world-readable systemd unit file ✅ Done. The installer had put it on the ExecStart line, where any local user could read it and it showed up in ps. It now lives in a root-only EnvironmentFile (chmod 600). I verified all 4 tunnel connections re-registered and every app still answered. It's the same secrets-in-arguments pattern I found in my auditd alert script.
  • [x] Narrowed the resume site's port binding ✅ Done. Docker publishes ports on every interface by default (and its iptables rules skip host firewalls). The port is now bound to the NAS's LAN IP only, with the tunnel route pointing at that address. Devices on my home network can still reach it directly. Details and the trade-offs in the resume site docs.
  • [ ] Do the same for other apps whose only client is cloudflared. Routes that point at the LAN IP (not localhost) have to be switched first, or they'll break.
  • [ ] Protect Vaultwarden's /admin page with an Access policy scoped to that path (the main vault has to stay open for its apps).
  • [ ] Turn on Cloudflare Access for other admin-style apps where clients don't need direct API access.
  • [ ] Re-audit routes and DNS records regularly. Today's findings were all drift: leftovers from setups that changed.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Zero Trust in practice: identity checked at the edge, default deny, and policies written as explicit conditions
  • Federating identity: connecting Cloudflare Access to my own Authentik over OpenID Connect (client IDs, redirect URIs, signing keys, JWKS)
  • Configuration drift is a real attack surface. None of the findings came from one big mistake. Old setups left things behind, and only an actual audit found them.
  • DNS reveals more than you think. One leftover record exposed what the whole tunnel was built to hide.
  • Verify, don't assume. Checking the authoritative nameservers (not a cache) told me whether the fix had really worked. Reading the DDNS container's logs proved my first theory wrong. Broken services can still be liabilities, so I removed it regardless.
  • Matching tools to protocols: HTTP through the tunnel, raw game traffic through playit.gg, private access over Tailscale or the LAN

docs.title: Dawarich
docs.text:
Self-hosted location history (Google Timeline replacement)

Host ShineoriServer Category Apps Status 🟢 running Exposed? Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports) Version 1.16.0 (pinned) Login Authentik SSO (OIDC), plus local password login

Compose file: stacks/dawarich/

🚚 Moved from ShiNAS to ShineoriServer in October 2026 to free up RAM on the NAS. Its database and files live in Docker named volumes, so this one needed a volume export and import, plus the laptop's IP added to APPLICATION_HOSTS. Full story: Moving services off the NAS.

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text: I like having a timeline of where I've been, like Google Timeline, but a record of everywhere I go is about as personal as data gets. Dawarich gives me the map, the visits and the stats while the location history stays on my own server instead of someone else's.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Dawarich is four containers on a private Docker network. Only the web app has a published port.

flowchart LR
    phone([Phone / browser]) --> cf[Cloudflare edge]
    cf --> tun[[Tunnel<br/>cloudflared on ShiNAS]]
    tun -- LAN --> app[dawarich_app<br/>Rails web app]
    app --> db[(dawarich_db<br/>PostgreSQL + PostGIS)]
    app --> redis[(dawarich_redis<br/>job queue)]
    sidekiq[dawarich_sidekiq<br/>background jobs] --> db
    sidekiq --> redis
    app -. OIDC login .-> ak[Authentik]
Container Job dawarich_app The web interface and API that receives location points dawarich_sidekiq Background work: imports, reverse geocoding, stats dawarich_db PostgreSQL with PostGIS, an extension for storing and querying map coordinates dawarich_redis The queue that hands jobs from the app to Sidekiq

Where the data lives: five Docker named volumes (db_data, storage, public, watched, shared), not the stack's folder. That matters when moving or backing it up (see the troubleshooting log).

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Published through the Cloudflare Tunnel Location data can arrive from anywhere, with no open router ports Login through Authentik (OIDC) One passkey login instead of another password (see Authentik) OIDC_AUTO_REGISTER: "false" Signing in with Authentik can't create new Dawarich accounts, only log in to existing ones Database has no published port PostgreSQL is only reachable by the other containers on the private Docker network APPLICATION_HOSTS allow-list The app only answers to the hostnames and addresses on this list Secrets in a git-ignored .env SECRET_KEY_BASE and the OIDC client secret. The repo only has a blanked .env.example.

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Put SECRET_KEY_BASE and DAWARICH_OIDC_SECRET in .env, plus APPLICATION_HOSTS with the public hostname and the server's LAN IP
  2. docker compose up -d and wait until all four containers report healthy
  3. Add a tunnel route: public hostname → http://<LAN_IP>:3009
  4. SSO: create an OAuth2/OIDC provider in Authentik with Dawarich's redirect URI. Dawarich needs a verified email claim, so the provider uses a custom scope mapping (see the troubleshooting log).
  5. Point the phone's location tracking at the public hostname
  6. Always start logins from the public hostname, not the IP (see the troubleshooting log)
  7. Health checks go to /api/v1/health, not /. Since 1.16.0, / redirects to the sign-in page.

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Date Problem Root cause Fix — SSO didn't work with Authentik's default scopes Dawarich is strict about the email claim it receives Built a custom email scope mapping in Authentik that marks the email as verified (details) 2026-10-11 Moving the stack folder alone would have produced an empty Dawarich All the data lives in Docker named volumes, not in the folder Exported each volume to a tarball with a throwaway container, created empty volumes on the new machine with docker compose create, then imported them. Checked PG_VERSION before starting. 2026-10-11 Needed the new machine's IP in APPLICATION_HOSTS Rails rejects requests for hosts that aren't on the allow-list Appended it to .env with a leading newline, so it couldn't get glued onto the end of SECRET_KEY_BASE 2026-10-11 Sign in with Authentik ended on a Cloudflare 502 The tunnel route still pointed at the old machine. I'd also started the login on the LAN IP, but Authentik sends you back to the public hostname, so the login cookie wouldn't have matched anyway. Repointed the tunnel route and started the login from the public hostname 2026-10-13 The web app was down for hours while the database and background worker were fine I'd rebooted the laptop. Docker stopped every container cleanly (exit code 0), and the web app and worker used the upstream restart: on-failure policy, which only restarts after a crash, so a clean stop left them down. Changed both to restart: unless-stopped, like every other app in the lab. Found the cause in the system journal: sudo reboot now at the exact second the app shut down. 2026-10-21 Upgrading 1.15.3 to 1.16.0 The release notes warned about a one-time background migration (merging duplicate legacy points and recalculating achievements) and that / now redirects to sign-in Diffed the upstream compose file between the two versions first: no changes. Backed up the stopped stack and all its volumes, bumped both image tags, then let the migration finish before judging anything. /api/v1/health answered {"status":"ok"}.

docs.text:
• [x] Backed up ✅ Done: nightly pg_dump plus its files, encrypted, to an append-only repository on the NAS. Restore tested. (Backups)
  • [ ] Replace the stock database credentials from the upstream compose file

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Named volumes vs bind mounts: where a container keeps its data decides how you back it up and move it. docker volume ls first, always.
  • PostGIS: a database can understand geography as well as numbers and text
  • Host allow-lists: web frameworks like Rails refuse requests for hostnames they weren't told about, which blocks a class of attacks but needs updating when a server moves
  • Read the release notes, then diff the compose file: the notes say what changes inside the app, the compose diff says whether my setup has to change too
  • OIDC flows are tied to addresses: the redirect URI and the login cookie both depend on the hostname, so mixing an IP and a domain breaks the login

docs.title: Diun (update notifications)
docs.text:
Watches every container image in the lab and pings Discord when a new stable version ships. It never installs anything by itself.

Host ShiNAS + ShineoriServer (one instance on each) Category Networking & monitoring Status 🟢 running Exposed? No. Outbound only (container registries, a Discord webhook, and my Hermes Agent on the LAN) Version 4.33.0 (pinned)

Compose file: stacks/diun/

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text:
Most of my apps used to float on :latest, which meant any docker compose pull could silently upgrade them. That includes breaking changes, and makes "what changed?" hard to answer when something breaks. So I made a two-part change:

  1. Pin every image to an exact version, so nothing changes until I decide.
  2. Run Diun, so pinning doesn't mean missing updates. It tells me when a new version exists, and I upgrade on my own schedule.
🔔 Diun (awareness)                     📌 Pinned images (control)
every 6h: check registries for     ──▶  "immich-server v3.3.2 is out" → Discord
new stable version tags                  read release notes → bump the tag → update
never installs anything                  roll back = change the tag back

docs.title: How the pinning was done (safely)
docs.text:
Pinning can go wrong if you guess a version number and accidentally change what's running. So I made it a verify-first process:

  1. Inventory: read the real version label from every running container (org.opencontainers.image.version)
  2. Verify: pull each proposed tag and compare its image ID with the running container's image. 14 of 14 matched, so every pin was byte-for-byte what was already running.
  3. Digest pins for 3 images with no usable version (one reported latest, another main): tag@sha256:<digest>, where the digest is the source of truth
  4. Apply with a script that backs up every file first, then validate every compose file (docker compose config -q)
  5. No restarts needed: the images were identical, so pinning changed nothing today, and only stops surprise changes tomorrow

Databases (Postgres, PostGIS, Redis/Valkey) stay locked to their major version, which is the usual convention. Major upgrades are the dangerous ones for databases, and those are already blocked.

docs.title: Configuration choices
docs.text: Setting Why WATCHREPO: true + NOTIFYON: new Pinned tags never change, so Diun has to look for new tags in each repository instead of watching the current one Include ^v?\d+\.\d+\.\d+ Only real version numbers, which skips the dozens of variant tags database images publish Exclude rc / beta / alpha / dev / nightly / pre Stable releases only FIRSTCHECKNOTIF: false The first scan quietly records what exists, instead of announcing every historical version Every 6 hours, 30s jitter Frequent enough to be useful, gentle on registry rate limits hostname: shinas / shineoriserver Each Discord notification says which server it's about, since Diun runs on both A separate Discord webhook and channel Update chatter stays out of my security-alerts channel, and either webhook can be revoked on its own Webhook in a root-only .env Entered with read -s, so it never touched the screen, my shell history, the compose file or git

docs.title: Least privilege: the socket proxy
docs.text:
I first thought mounting the Docker socket :ro made it "look but don't touch". That's wrong. :ro only stops the socket file from being replaced. The Docker API behind it stays fully available, and the Docker engine runs as root, so socket access means root on the host.

The fix is a socket proxy: a tiny container that holds the real socket and only forwards the requests I allow.

flowchart LR
    d[Diun] -- "tcp :2375<br/>private network" --> p[socket-proxy<br/>CONTAINERS=1 · IMAGES=1 · POST=0]
    p -- "read-only API calls only" --> s[(docker.sock)]
    d -- internet --> r[Registries + Discord]
Design choice Why Proxy allows CONTAINERS + IMAGES, POST=0 Diun only needs to read which images are running. Every change (create, start, stop, delete) is denied. Proxy sits on an internal: true network No ports and no internet. Only Diun can reach it. Diun has no socket mount at all Even if Diun were compromised, the worst it could do is list containers Proxy pinned by digest Same rule as everything else: nothing changes by surprise

Proven, not assumed. I tested it from a throwaway container on the proxy's network:

READ  (list containers):  200   ✅ allowed
WRITE (create container): 403   ✅ blocked
Diun has the socket?      0     ✅ not mounted

I also removed the socket from Authentik's worker entirely, since it never needed it. That means two apps no longer have root-equivalent access to the NAS.

docs.title: Update Scout: release notes read for me
docs.text:
Each Diun instance has a second notifier: a webhook to Hermes Agent, my local AI agent. For every new version, Hermes finds the version I'm running, reads the release notes in between, and posts a 🟢 / 🟡 / 🔴 verdict in Discord a few minutes later.

Setting Why DIUN_NOTIF_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT → Hermes on port 8644 LAN only. The port is never published through a tunnel DIUN_NOTIF_WEBHOOK_METHOD=POST + JSON content type Hermes reads the image, host and container name from the body DIUN_NOTIF_WEBHOOK_HEADERS_X-GITLAB-TOKEN Hermes requires every webhook to be authenticated. Diun can't sign requests, but it can send a fixed header, and Hermes accepts a GitLab-style shared token Lives in the same root-only .env as the Discord webhook Same rule: secrets never touch the compose file or git

diun notif test now fires both notifiers. The test image is latest, so the right answer from Hermes is "can't scout a floating tag", and that's what it says.

docs.title: How I apply an update
docs.text:
Diun only tells me; I do the update by hand:

1. read     → Hermes's verdict, then the release notes it links (look for "breaking changes", and be extra careful with major versions)
2. check    → the version I'm actually running:
              docker inspect --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version"}}' <container>
3. backup   → make sure that night's backup ran, or run one now
4. bump     → change the tag in the compose file (keep a .bak copy of the old file)
5. apply    → docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
6. verify   → logs are clean, the app opens, the data is there
7. record   → update the stack and docs in this repo

Rolling back is putting the old tag back, unless the new version migrated the app's database. That's why step 3 comes before step 5.

Problems I've hit:

  • Version labels aren't always versions. Homarr's label said main (a code branch). Comparing the image's build date with the release dates told me which version it really was.
  • Images on :latest update themselves whenever their stack restarts. SearXNG was already on the version Diun announced, so I pinned it.
  • Some apps' data is tied to their version. Meilisearch can't open data from a much older release, but it's only Karakeep's search index, so I rebuilt the index instead of migrating it. I also upgraded to the version Karakeep recommends (v1.41.0), not the newest one Diun announced (v1.55.0): for a dependency, the app that uses it decides the version.

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Problem Root cause Fix 403 Forbidden listing tags for Karakeep's headless-Chrome image That image lives on a Google registry that doesn't allow anonymous tag listing Added the label diun.enable=false to that one service. It's pinned (124) and rarely updated. Later, the same image couldn't be downloaded at all when I moved Karakeep to my second server The Google registry project hosting it stopped serving downloads ("billing must be enabled"). It only kept working where it was already downloaded. Switched to the same image on Docker Hub (docker.io/zenika/alpine-chrome:124). Lesson: an image that runs fine today can become impossible to download again.

docs.title: What I'd harden next
docs.text:
• [x] Put a docker-socket-proxy in front of the Docker socket ✅ Done (see below).
  • [x] Added Diun to ShineoriServer ✅ Done: the same compose file, downloaded straight from this repo, with hostname: shineoriserver so each Discord alert says which machine it's about. Same socket proxy, same #updates channel, and a test notification confirmed it works.
  • [x] Automatic release-note review ✅ Done: a second notifier sends each new version to Hermes Agent, which posts a safe / read first / migration needed verdict
  • [ ] A monthly "update day": work through the Discord notifications and Hermes's verdicts, and bump the pins

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Pinning is configuration management: the compose files now describe exactly what runs, so a rebuild reproduces it
  • Verify before you change: comparing image IDs proved the pins were no-ops before I applied them
  • Tags vs digests: a tag is a movable label, and a digest is the content's fingerprint
  • Read-only isn't always read-only: :ro on a socket protects the file, not the API behind it. I caught my own wrong assumption while writing this page, fixed it with a socket proxy, and proved the fix with a 403.

docs.title: Flowcase
docs.text:
Browser-based isolated workspaces (Kasm-style), routed through ProtonVPN

Host ShiNAS Category Apps Status ⏸️ on demand (started only when I need it) Exposed? LAN only Port 8480

Compose file: stacks/flowcase/

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text: Sometimes I want a throwaway browser: to open a sketchy link, test something, or browse without my own IP showing. Flowcase spins up a disposable desktop or browser in a container, streams it to my browser, and deletes it afterwards. VPN workspaces send their traffic out through ProtonVPN, so sites see the VPN's IP, not my home's.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    me([Me, on the LAN]) --> nginx[flowcase-nginx<br/>:8480]
    nginx --> web[flowcase-web<br/>creates workspaces]
    web -- Docker API --> ws[Workspace containers]
    nginx --> ws
    ws -- flowcase_vpn network --> gluetun[flowcase-gluetun<br/>ProtonVPN WireGuard]
    gluetun --> net((Internet))
    fw[vpn-firewall<br/>host rules] -. blocks workspaces from .-> lan[NAS · LAN · other containers]
Container Job flowcase-web The app: logins, workspace templates, and starting and stopping workspace containers flowcase-nginx The front door. Routes each session to its workspace. On start it also deletes leftover routing configs for workspaces that no longer exist. flowcase-gluetun The VPN exit for workspaces on the isolated flowcase_vpn network vpn-firewall Host firewall rules so VPN workspaces can't reach the NAS, my LAN or other containers

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why VPN workspaces on their own network (10.77.77.0/24) Their only way out is through gluetun Host firewall around that network A compromised workspace (that's the whole point of a throwaway browser) can't pivot to the NAS or my home network LAN only and on demand It was published through the tunnel at first; it doesn't need to be on the internet, so it isn't. It also only runs when I'm using it. Accepted risk: Docker socket flowcase-web mounts the Docker socket because it has to create containers. That's effectively root on the NAS, which is a big part of why Flowcase stays LAN only and off when unused. Accepted risk: privileged firewall container vpn-firewall needs privileged and the host network to load kernel modules and set firewall rules

docs.text:
1. Clone Flowcase; my real configuration is the override files in this repo (docker-compose.nas.yml, plus the VPN pieces)
  2. Put a ProtonVPN WireGuard private key in vpn.env (Proton account → Downloads → WireGuard configuration)
  3. docker compose -f docker-compose.nas.yml up -d
  4. Open http://<LAN_IP>:8480, create the admin account, add workspace templates, and attach VPN templates to the flowcase_vpn network
  5. docker compose stop when finished

docs.text: Date Problem Root cause Fix — nginx could fail to start after a restart Leftover routing configs pointed at workspace containers that no longer existed, and nginx refuses to start when it can't resolve a host in its config nginx's start command now deletes configs whose workspace container can't be found
