    ts --> srv[The Forest dedicated server<br/>Windows 11 · SteamCMD]
    srv --> cfg[(server.cfg<br/>ports, slots, settings)]
Port Use 8766 Steam 27015 Game 27020 Query (moved from its default, see the troubleshooting log)

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Tailscale instead of port forwarding Only friends on my private Tailscale network could reach it; nothing was open to the internet serverIP set to the Tailscale address The server listened on the private network, not the public one Anonymous Steam account No Steam login stored on the server

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Install SteamCMD and download the dedicated server with it
  2. Edit server.cfg: ports, 4 slots, serverIP set to the machine's Tailscale address
  3. Make sure the server is launched with that config file (see below)
  4. Friends join over Tailscale

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Date Problem Root cause Fix 2026-09 The server crashed about 2 seconds after every launch, with an access violation in CSteamworks.dll It was loading the wrong config file. With the stale settings, the query port was already in use, so Steam's server initialisation failed and left the game with a broken Steam interface, which crashed it. Pointed the server at the correct config and moved the query port to 27020

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Root cause over symptoms: the crash was in a Steam DLL, but the real cause was one step earlier, a config file being read from the wrong place
  • Read the startup sequence: port in use → Steam init fails → crash later. Following that chain found the fix.
  • Private networking with Tailscale as an alternative to opening ports

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text:
Uptime monitoring and alerts for every service

Host ShineoriServer Category Networking & monitoring Status 🟢 running Exposed? LAN only Port 3001

Compose file: stacks/uptime-kuma/

🚚 Moved from ShiNAS to ShineoriServer in October 2026 to free up RAM on the NAS. From there it watches the NAS from the outside, including a ping monitor for the NAS itself, so it can report when the NAS goes down instead of going down with it. Full story: Moving services off the NAS.

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text: With services spread across two machines, I needed one place that tells me what's up, what's down, and since when, instead of finding out when an app doesn't load. Uptime Kuma checks every service every minute and keeps a history, so I can spot problems early and see patterns (like everything failing at the same moment).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    me([Me, on the LAN]) --> kuma[Uptime Kuma<br/>ShineoriServer]
    kuma -- HTTP checks --> nas[Apps on ShiNAS]
    kuma -- HTTP checks --> laptop[Apps on ShineoriServer]
    kuma -- ping --> host[ShiNAS itself]
    kuma --> db[(./data<br/>kuma.db SQLite)]
    homarr[Homarr dashboard] -- status page --> kuma
Piece Job Monitors One HTTP check per web app, using the machine's LAN address (never localhost), plus a ping check for the NAS Tags Group related monitors, like the arr tag for the media-automation apps Status page A read-only page that Homarr reads to show live status on my dashboard ./data Everything (settings, monitors, history) lives in one SQLite database in a bind-mounted folder

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why LAN only It isn't published through the tunnel. It shows the layout of my whole lab, which doesn't need to be on the internet. Status pages are public by design Anyone who can reach the app can view a status page without logging in. That's fine on the LAN, but it's a reason to think before ever publishing it. Runs on a different machine than most of what it watches So a NAS outage gets reported instead of taking the monitor down too Image pinned to major version 2 Updates within v2 only, no surprise major upgrade

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. docker compose up -d with ./data mounted to /app/data
  2. Create the admin account on first visit to http://<LAN_IP>:3001
  3. Add monitors using LAN IPs, not localhost or container names, so they keep working no matter which machine Uptime Kuma runs on
  4. Pause monitors for on-demand services (Flowcase, Ghiro) so only real outages show red
  5. Create a status page for the Homarr widget
  6. Moving it: stop the container first, then copy the folder. Stopping merges SQLite's write-ahead log (kuma.db-wal) into kuma.db, so the copy isn't half-saved.

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Date Problem Root cause Fix 2026-10-11 "Cannot connect to the socket server" Not Uptime Kuma itself: the whole NAS was overloaded by Immich (diagnosis), and Uptime Kuma ran on that same NAS Fixed the overload, then moved Uptime Kuma to the other machine so it can report the next one 2026-10-11 12 monitors red at once, burying anything real Services I'd stopped on purpose (on-demand apps, things paused during the overload) still had active monitors Paused monitors for services that are meant to be off 2026-10-11 Couldn't log in after the move I'd forgotten the admin password Reset it inside the container with npm run reset-password. Monitors and history are untouched. It's in my password manager now. 2026-10-11 Homarr's Uptime Kuma widget returned 404 Homarr reads a status page, and with no slug set it asks for one called default, which didn't exist Created a status page and gave Homarr its slug

docs.title: What I'd harden next
docs.text:
• [ ] Discord notifications on the important monitors, so an outage reaches my phone
  • [ ] A push monitor as a dead-man's switch for the nightly backup (alerts if the backup doesn't run at all)
  • [ ] Monitors for NAS load and swap, to catch the next overload before apps time out

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Monitoring belongs outside what it monitors. When the NAS overloaded, the monitor running on it went down too instead of warning me.
  • Alert fatigue is real. A dashboard with 12 expected reds hides the one unexpected red, so "intentionally off" needs to look different from "broken".
  • Design for moving: monitors that use LAN addresses survived the move to a new machine without a single edit
  • SQLite's write-ahead log: recent changes can live in a separate -wal file, so you stop the app before copying its database

docs.title: Vaultwarden
docs.text:
My own password manager server: passwords, TOTP codes and passkeys, under my control and portable across devices

Host ShiNAS Category Security & identity Status 🟢 running Exposed? Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports) Version 1.37.3 (pinned)

Compose file: stacks/vaultwarden/

docs.title: Why I run it
docs.text:
I wanted every credential (passwords, 2FA codes and passkeys) in one place that I control and can take with me. Passkeys in particular tend to get locked into one phone's ecosystem. If they live in my own Bitwarden-compatible vault instead, a new phone, or even a switch between iPhone and Android, can't strand them.

Vaultwarden is a lightweight, Rust-based server that speaks the Bitwarden API. So I get the official Bitwarden apps and browser extensions on every device, backed by a server running on my NAS.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    apps([Bitwarden apps<br/>phone · browser · desktop]) --> cf[Cloudflare edge<br/>HTTPS]
    cf --> tun[[Cloudflare Tunnel]]
    tun --> vw[Vaultwarden<br/>container]
    vw --> data[(vw-data/<br/>SQLite + attachments)]

docs.title: The security model: zero-knowledge
docs.text:
The most important thing about this service is what the server can't do:

📱 device:  master password → derives key → encrypts vault locally
                                                   │
                                                   ▼  only encrypted blobs travel
🗄️ server:  stores ciphertext it cannot read, plus a hash to check logins

Encryption and decryption happen on my devices. Vaultwarden only ever stores encrypted data. Even if someone stole the whole vw-data/ folder, they'd still need my master password to read anything. Exposing it through the tunnel is a reasonable trade-off because of this. It's the same model Bitwarden's own cloud uses.

docs.title: Security decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Invite-only registration Public sign-ups are off. Friends join through an invite to my Bitwarden organization, which also lets us share logins like the Wi-Fi password. Strangers who find the URL can't create accounts (see the troubleshooting log). Admin panel disabled No ADMIN_TOKEN is set, so /admin shows a "disabled" page and there's no admin login to brute-force Published through Cloudflare Tunnel No open router ports, home IP hidden, HTTPS at the edge Not behind Cloudflare Access The Bitwarden apps talk to the API directly and can't complete a browser login challenge. The vault's own encryption and master password are the protection here. Email through a dedicated homelab mailbox Invites, new-device login alerts and 2FA-by-email go out from a homelab-only Gmail account, never my personal email. It uses STARTTLS on port 587. A separate app password per service Vaultwarden has its own Gmail app password, not shared with Authentik, so if one leaks I can revoke it without breaking anything else SMTP secrets in a root-only .env Credentials live in .env (chmod 600, root-owned), loaded with env_file. The compose file holds no secrets, and the repo has a blanked .env.example. DOMAIN set to the public HTTPS URL Vaultwarden needs this for attachments and passkeys (WebAuthn) to work behind a proxy

docs.title: Setup notes
docs.text:
1. Start the container: docker compose up -d (data persists in ./vw-data)
  2. Publish it through the tunnel and set DOMAIN to the public https:// URL
  3. Create my account, then set SIGNUPS_ALLOWED: "false" and recreate the container
  4. Email: create a Gmail app password for the homelab alerts account and write the SMTP_* settings to a root-only .env (I read the password with read -s so it never appears on screen or in shell history). Add env_file: .env to the compose file, recreate the container, and test it with Get master password hint.
  5. Create an Organization in the web vault and invite friends by email. They get a Join organization link and can register even though public sign-ups are off.
  6. Point the Bitwarden apps at the self-hosted server URL (Settings → Self-hosted)
  7. Import passwords, then move 2FA codes and passkeys in over time

docs.title: Troubleshooting log
docs.text: Problem Root cause Fix Public sign-ups were still open on an internet-facing server. Found while documenting the setup. SIGNUPS_ALLOWED stayed "true" after I created my account, even though the compose file's own comment says to turn it off Switched to invite-only: SIGNUPS_ALLOWED: "false" with invitations still allowed. Recreated the container and verified from outside. After the fix, the server's public config still reported registration as not disabled That flag stays on while invitations are allowed, so invited users can still reach the sign-up page. It isn't proof that strangers can register. Tested the real behavior instead: an uninvited address trying to start registration gets 400 Registration not allowed.

docs.title: What I'd harden next
docs.text:
• [x] Pinned the image version ✅ Done: 1.37.3 instead of :latest, verified identical to the running image. Diun announces new releases in Discord.
  • [ ] The NAS's network share can read root-only files. While syncing configs, my collector (connecting over the share) could read this chmod 600 root .env, so whatever account the share uses bypasses those permissions. Fix: scope the share to a non-admin account, or exclude secret files from it.
  • [x] Nightly encrypted backups ✅ Done: consistent SQLite snapshot + rsa_key + attachments, backed up to an encrypted restic repository on a second disk. The restore is tested: 548 of 548 items and 4 of 4 users matched, and the integrity check passed. See Backups.
  • [ ] Replicate those backups off the NAS (second server, then off-site)
  • [ ] Keep an offline emergency kit: master password plus the 2FA recovery code for my vault account, stored on paper somewhere safe
  • [ ] Check the brute-force protections on the login endpoint, and alert on failed logins
  • [x] Configured SMTP ✅ Done: invitations and new-device login alerts now arrive by email, sent through the lab's alerts mailbox with a dedicated app password

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Zero-knowledge architecture: why a password manager can be internet-facing when the server never holds decryption keys
  • The gap between "set up" and "secured": a one-time step (closing sign-ups) is easy to forget once everything works. Auditing your own setup catches it.
  • Verifying from the attacker's side: a status flag said one thing, but testing what a stranger can actually do said another. Behavior beats indicators.
  • Handling secrets during setup: a password typed with read -s into a chmod 600 file never touches the screen, my shell history, the compose file or git. I confirmed it was written correctly from the file size alone, without ever looking at it.
  • Passkey portability: where credentials live matters as much as how strong they are
